openings.claim: An ordinary bolted strip clamp with cork contact pads may retain either plate while allowing screwdriver release and gloved removal by an unmarked edge.
openings.delta: Change retention dependence from magnetic attraction to screw-loaded contact carried by drilled steel strips bolted through the existing carriage slots. Use only supplied strips, bolts and pads; place every contact outside the working edge and stroke clearance. Slot compatibility and usable clamp geometry remain unknown.
openings.prediction: If the slots accept the bolts and the strips can clamp a supported nonworking region, the spare plate should remain within 1 mm after twenty strokes and permit removal and return within sixty seconds. The nearest rival is magnet retention: the supplied 3 N versus 7 N pull difference suggests sensitivity to plate substitution. Mechanical clamping should show less substitution sensitivity, but neither retention nor timing is established.
openings.probe: First check slot fit and clearance with the ruler before fabrication; reject this arrangement if compliant placement is impossible. Within eighty minutes, fabricate one clamp configuration using at most four strips, six bolts and four pads. Within twenty observation minutes, run up to three twenty-stroke checks, including the spare plate for the final run; measure displacement from carriage reference marks. Perform up to three timed removal/return checks, including the final spare removal in thick gloves, handling only unmarked regions. If time remains, compare original and spare release force under equal clamp settings up to the 10 N scale limit; do not infer forces beyond it.
assumptions: The mounting slots accept supplied M4 fasteners without carriage modification.
The carriage supports compliant strip placement and screwdriver access.
Available strip stiffness and achievable preload resist the unspecified stroke loads.

assessment: Defeat conditions are displacement above 1 mm, service time above sixty seconds, working-edge contact, clearance intrusion, or inability to fabricate using the supplied resources and time. Unknown geometry and loads prevent a feasibility claim; this is a probe, not deployment.
